articles.title: Why your CI keeps creating iOS certificates (and how to stop it)
articles.excerpt: I'm on the MacBuildCloud team. We run Mac build machines, and this is a bug we shipped into our own pipeline and then took back out. Nothing here depends on our product; every fix below works on GitHu…
articles.body: I'm on the MacBuildCloud team. We run Mac build machines, and this is a bug we shipped into our own pipeline and then took back out. Nothing here depends on our product; every fix below works on GitHub Actions, a self-hosted runner, or any CI that throws its Mac away after each job. The symptom Open developer.apple.com, go to Certificates , and look for entries named like this: Apple Development: Created via API If you see one you don't remember making, and especially if you see several, there is a good chance a CI job made them. We found ours during our own TestFlight test. The build passed. The .ipa was fine. Then we checked the team's certificate list and there was a new development certificate that nobody had asked for.
articles.author: MacBuildCloud

articles.title: The palletizing cell already knows why it stopped — if you log the right things
articles.excerpt: Every palletizing cell I have ever walked up to had an opinion about why it loses time. The operator had one ("the wrapper upstream is slow"), the shift leader had another ("changeovers eat the mornin…
articles.body: Every palletizing cell I have ever walked up to had an opinion about why it loses time. The operator had one ("the wrapper upstream is slow"), the shift leader had another ("changeovers eat the morning"), and the PLC, quietly, had the real one — recorded in a fault register nobody had opened in months. End-of-line data logging is not an Industry 4.0 luxury. It is the difference between arguing about downtime and fixing it. This is the logging setup I now treat as the minimum on a palletizing cell, and what each record is actually for. Log stops as events, not as a single downtime number A cell that reports "47 minutes of downtime" has told you almost nothing. What you need is a list of stop events: timestamp, duration, and a cause code chosen at restart.

articles.excerpt: Checkers looks like the easy one. Eight by eight board, pieces move diagonally, jump to capture, reach the far side and you get a king. It's one of the classics on mympgames, my free browser arcade. T…
articles.body: Checkers looks like the easy one. Eight by eight board, pieces move diagonally, jump to capture, reach the far side and you get a king. It's one of the classics on mympgames , my free browser arcade. The board is the simple part. Two rules carry most of the complexity: captures are mandatory , and a capture that can continue must continue with the same piece . Get either wrong and the game quietly stops being checkers. This post walks through the rules module the server uses, with the real code (trimmed a bit), and the decisions behind it.

articles.title: ffmpeg full to limited range: out_range=limited did nothing on yuvj420p until format=yuv420p went in
articles.excerpt: A filter chain that says scale=out_range=limited,setparams=range=tv, with -color_range tv on the output, reads like a finished job: convert a full-range H.264 file to limited range and label it that w…
articles.body: A filter chain that says scale=out_range=limited,setparams=range=tv , with -color_range tv on the output, reads like a finished job: convert a full-range H.264 file to limited range and label it that way. In this run it did neither. The source decoded as yuvj420p , and the encoded file came back as yuvj420p with color_range=pc , its pixel values not converted. One change fixed it. With format=yuv420p inserted after the scale, the next encode probed as yuv420p and tv , and its luma ran from 15 to 235. With -v error nothing was printed and the command looked complete, which worries me more than the bug itself. The test file and how far the result goes One Apple-silicon Mac, ffmpeg and ffprobe 9.0.2, each command run once.
articles.author: hao jia

articles.title: US cities have some of the world’s weakest indoor mobile signals, Ookla finds
articles.excerpt: Better indoor reception starts with better outdoor coverage.
articles.body: TL;DR A new Ookla study ranks North America among the worst-performing regions globally for indoor 4G signal strength. Weak indoor signals affect 41% of measured buildings in Miami, 38% in Los Angeles, and 25% in New York, compared to just 2% in Seoul. Weak outdoor coverage explains about 85% of the differences in indoor signal strength between cities, although dedicated in-building cellular equipment can significantly improve reception. Much has been made of the strides US carriers have made in improving their networks, with recent reports highlighting everything from faster download speeds to wider 5G coverage . But those improvements may not mean much when you’re struggling to upload a photo from your living room.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.body: On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: Relive Starship’s historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and ‘Mechazilla’ tower catch
articles.excerpt: See the most epic photos from SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and historic launch tower catch.
articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.
articles.author: Josh Dinner

articles.body: California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday , Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a "dangerous product without proper oversight," as reported earlier by Reuters . The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face "was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability." articles.body: Sam… thank you. | Image: Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. "I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer," Altman said today. "I think the home tinkering is great."
